findings.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — Exact, case-sensitive lookup lets blocked email addresses bypass validation by changing letter case, especially in the case-insensitive domain portion

lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — BlockedEmail.should_block? records match statistics inside User validation, so the write is rolled back when the blocked email causes User#save to fail and blocked attempts are not recorded
app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — match_count += 1 followed by save is a non-atomic read-modify-write that can lose increments under concurrent matches

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: app/models/blocked_email.rb:13 — match_count += 1 followed by save is a non-atomic read-modify-write that can lose increments under concurrent matches
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core issue: the should_block_email? method has problematic side effects (updating match_count and saving) during what should be a read operation. The golden comment frames it as 'side effects during a read operation' causing race conditions, while the candidate frames it as 'non-atomic read-modify-write that can lose increments under concurrent matches'. Both are pointing to the same race condition/concurrency problem with the statistics update in this method.
